ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026, Section 2: Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes. Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1):S27-S49
ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026, Section 6: Glycemic Goals, Hypoglycemia, and Hyperglycemic Crises. Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1):S132-S149
ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026, Section 10: Cardiovascular Disease and Risk Management. Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1):S216-S245

notes: Text is paraphrased/structured, not verbatim. ADA licence prohibits text/data mining and redistribution without written permission: obtain permission (permissions@diabetes.org) before commercial deployment.
Prices are US AWP/NADAC (15 July 2025) from Table 9.3/9.4: relative cost only; replace with Indian market prices.
Decision support only: a licensed clinician must confirm every recommendation against the patient and current product labels.
Evidence grades A/B/C/E are the ADA grades attached to each recommendation.

patient_fields.notes: hemoglobinopathy, G6PD, HIV, pregnancy, CKD/dialysis, anemia, transfusion

recommendations.summary: Most adults with T1D: CSII or multiple daily injections of basal + prandial insulin (injected or inhaled).
Prefer insulin analogs (or inhaled insulin) over human insulin in T1D to reduce hypoglycemia.
Teach carb/fat/protein-matched mealtime dosing, correction doses, trend-based adjustment, sick-day and exercise management.
Reassess insulin plan and insulin-taking behavior every 3-6 months.
Use shared decision-making; weigh efficacy, CV/kidney/weight effects, hypoglycemia, cost/access, tolerability, preference.
Consider initial combination therapy to reach goals sooner.
T2D with ASCVD or high ASCVD risk: include GLP-1 RA and/or SGLT2i with proven CV benefit irrespective of A1C.
T2D with HF (HFrEF or HFpEF): SGLT2i irrespective of A1C.
T2D + obesity + symptomatic HFpEF: dual GIP/GLP-1 RA (tirzepatide) with proven benefit.
T2D + obesity + symptomatic HFpEF: GLP-1 RA (semaglutide) with proven symptom/HF-event benefit.
T2D with CKD (eGFR 20-60 and/or albuminuria): SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA with proven benefit. SGLT2i glucose-lowering weaker at eGFR <45.
eGFR <30: GLP-1 RA preferred (low hypoglycemia, CV benefit). Dialysis: GLP-1-based therapy not dependent on kidney clearance can be started/continued (grade C).
T2D + MASLD + overweight/obesity: GLP-1 RA with MASH benefit (A) or dual GIP/GLP-1 RA (B).
Biopsy-proven MASH or high fibrosis risk: GLP-1 RA preferred (A); pioglitazone or dual GIP/GLP-1 RA can be considered (B).
Pioglitazone + GLP-1 RA combination can be considered in MASH/high fibrosis risk.
Re-evaluate medication plan and taking behavior every 3-6 months.
Do not delay intensification/deintensification when goals are unmet.
Choose changes by glycemic and weight goals, comorbidities and hypoglycemia risk.
When adding a new agent, reassess need/dose of sulfonylureas, meglitinides and insulin.
Do not combine DPP-4 inhibitor with GLP-1 RA or dual GIP/GLP-1 RA (no added benefit).
If weight goals unmet add weight-management interventions (lifestyle, programs, drugs, metabolic surgery).
Consider insulin regardless of background therapy if symptomatic hyperglycemia, A1C >10% (>86 mmol/mol) or glucose >=300 mg/dL (>=16.7 mmol/L).
Without severe hyperglycemia/crisis, prefer GLP-1-based therapy over insulin for initial or add-on injectable.
If insulin is used, combine with GLP-1 RA/dual agonist; reassess insulin dose when GLP-1 RA is added or escalated.
When starting insulin continue other glucose-lowering agents unless contraindicated/not tolerated.
Healthy behaviors, DSMES, avoiding therapeutic inertia and SDOH are essential parts of every glucose-lowering plan.
Offer CGM at onset and any time to adults on insulin (A), on hypoglycemia-causing non-insulin drugs (B), or when CGM aids management (B).
Watch for bedtime-to-morning or post- to pre-prandial glucose differential, hypoglycemia, variability; re-evaluate promptly.
Offer automated insulin delivery to adults with T1D or T2D on insulin per preference.
Prescribe glucagon to everyone on insulin or at high hypoglycemia risk; teach family/caregivers; prefer no-reconstitution products (B).
Routinely screen for financial barriers and act to reduce cost.
With cost barriers consider lower-cost drugs (metformin, sulfonylurea, TZD, human insulin) weighing their risks.
Do not use non-FDA-approved compounded products (incl. incretins).
If a drug is unavailable switch to another approved agent with similar efficacy.
When supply returns reassess whether to resume original drug.
Counsel people of childbearing potential on contraception and drug effects on contraceptive efficacy.
Shared preconception planning: glycemic goals, timing of stopping non-insulin drugs, optimal glycemic management.
Hyperglycemia on PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors: assess urgently for insulin need (DKA risk).
Metformin first-line for mTOR-inhibitor hyperglycemia.
Metformin first-line for PI3K-alpha inhibitor hyperglycemia.
Reserve insulin for severe hyperglycemia/crisis in PI3K-inhibitor therapy.
Match glucose-lowering therapy to the steroid regimen; reassess frequently.
Post-transplant diabetes/T2D: insulin preferred postoperatively; DPP-4i for mild hyperglycemia.
Non-insulin agents usable long term; choice depends on organ.
GLP-1 RA can be considered long term for cardiometabolic benefit.
Add insulin if goals not met with non-insulin therapy.
Educate at-risk SGLT-inhibitor users on DKA signs and mitigation, give ketone (beta-hydroxybutyrate) testing tools, discourage ketogenic diets.
Advise all people with diabetes to participate in DSMES.
Provide DSMES at diagnosis, annually/when goals unmet, when complications arise, and at life/care transitions.
Assess outcomes, health status and well-being on an individual timeframe.
Use motivational interviewing, goal setting and problem-solving.
Culturally/socially appropriate group or individual DSMES; share participation with the care team.
Offer DSMES via telehealth/digital interventions.
DSMES improves outcomes and reduces cost: payor reimbursement recommended.
Identify and address barriers to DSMES.
Assess social determinants to design DSMES.
Refer to a registered dietitian (RDN) for individualized MNT.
MNT saves cost and improves cardiometabolic outcomes: should be reimbursed.
Overweight/obesity: treatment plan aiming for at least 5-7% weight loss.
Individualized meal plans considering nutrient quality, calories, metabolic goals.
Emphasize non-starchy vegetables, whole fruit, legumes, lean protein, whole grains, nuts/seeds, low-fat dairy; minimize red meat, sugary drinks, sweets, refined grains, ultra-processed food.
Consider reducing carbohydrate in some adults, best by limiting processed foods.
Micronutrient or herbal supplements (magnesium, chromium, cinnamon, aloe) not recommended for glycemia; ask about use.
Counsel against beta-carotene supplements.
Do not exceed recommended limits (<=1 drink/day women, <=2 men); abstainers should not start.
Counsel on delayed hypoglycemia and glucose monitoring after alcohol, esp. on insulin/secretagogues.
Limit sodium to <2,300 mg/day as clinically appropriate.
Encourage water over other beverages.
Non-nutritive sweeteners acceptable in moderation, short term, in place of sugar.
Monitor nutrition adequacy (protein, micronutrients) during intentional weight loss.
Choose minimally processed, high-fiber carbohydrate (>=14 g fiber per 1,000 kcal).
Replace sugar-sweetened drinks (incl. juices) with water/low- or no-calorie drinks.
SGLT-inhibitor users: ketoacidosis education, ketone tools, avoid ketogenic eating.
Teach glycemic impact of carbohydrate, fat and protein for mealtime insulin dosing.
Fixed-dose insulin: keep consistent carbohydrate timing/amount.
More plant-based protein (nuts, seeds, legumes).
Consider Mediterranean-style eating pattern.
Limit saturated fat.
Religious fasting: use IDF-DAR risk assessment and fasting-focused education.
Assess and optimize treatment plan, dose and timing well before fasting.
Assess baseline activity/sedentary time; encourage increase; break sitting every 30 min.
Children/adolescents: >=60 min/day moderate-vigorous activity, strengthening >=3 days/week, limit screen time.
Adults: >=150 min/week moderate-vigorous aerobic over >=3 days, no >2 consecutive inactive days (75 min vigorous may suffice if fit).
Resistance exercise 2-3 sessions/week on non-consecutive days.
Older adults: flexibility and balance training 2-3 times/week.
On obesity drugs/after metabolic surgery: prioritize muscle-strengthening to preserve lean mass.
Ask about tobacco/vaping every visit; advise complete avoidance; provide counseling + pharmacotherapy.
T1D and others at DKA risk: advise against recreational cannabis.
Provide psychosocial care to all people with diabetes.
Screen at least annually and with changes in health/treatment/life.
Refer to behavioral health professionals when indicated.
Screen for diabetes distress at least annually.
Screen for anxiety annually.
Screen those at high hypoglycemia risk annually; refer for evidence-based intervention.
Screen for depression at least annually.
Rescreen at complication diagnosis or major change in status.
Screen with validated tools; review treatment for effects on hunger/intake.
Reevaluate treatment plan with a qualified professional if disordered eating is present.
Provide enhanced monitoring/support for diabetes self-management.
Monitor weight, glycemia, lipids on second-generation antipsychotics.
Monitor cognitive capacity across the life span.
Refer for formal assessment if cognition suboptimal for self-management.
Screen sleep health and sleep disorders; refer as needed.
Counsel on sleep-promoting routines.
Monitor prediabetes for progression at least annually.
A1C about every 6 months and 75-g OGTT annually.
Refer overweight/obese high-risk adults to a diabetes prevention program: >=5-7% weight loss, >=150 min/week activity.
Prescribe evidence-based eating pattern (e.g., Mediterranean, low-carbohydrate) in prediabetes.
Offer DPP to high-risk adults; payors should cover.
Certified technology-assisted DPPs are an option.
Consider metformin for high risk: age 25-59, BMI >=35, FPG >=110 mg/dL, A1C >=6.0%, or prior GDM.
Consider metformin to prevent hyperglycemia on PI3K-alpha inhibitors.
Consider metformin to prevent hyperglycemia in high-risk people on high-dose glucocorticoids.
Periodically check vitamin B12 on long-term metformin (esp. anemia/neuropathy).
Prediabetes raises CV risk: screen and treat modifiable risk factors.
Statins may raise diabetes risk: monitor glucose, reinforce prevention, do not stop statins for this reason.
Prior stroke + insulin resistance/prediabetes: pioglitazone may be considered; weigh weight gain, edema, fractures.
Care goals: weight loss/maintenance, limit glycemic progression, CV risk attention.
Consider pharmacotherapy to support person-centered goals.
More intensive prevention if BMI >=35, FPG 110-125, 2-h glucose 173-199, A1C >=6.0%, or prior GDM.
Discuss teplizumab with selected people aged >=8 years with stage 2 T1D.
Diagnose diabetes by A1C, fasting glucose, 2-h OGTT glucose, or random glucose >=200 mg/dL with classic symptoms/crisis.
Without unequivocal hyperglycemia, confirm with a second abnormal test (same or different test).
Use NGSP-certified A1C method traceable to DCCT.
Point-of-care A1C for diagnosis only with FDA-approved devices in CLIA-certified labs.
Investigate interference when glucose and A1C are consistently discordant.
Use plasma glucose criteria with hemoglobin variants, pregnancy, G6PD deficiency, HIV, altered red-cell turnover.
Classify hyperglycemia into diagnostic category to guide therapy.
Screen presymptomatic T1D with islet autoantibodies (insulin, GAD, IA-2, ZnT8).
Offer autoantibody screening to people with family history or elevated genetic risk.
Autoantibody-positive: test for stage 3 T1D (A1C, urinalysis, glucose).
Multiple autoantibodies: refer to specialist center for staging, education, teplizumab/trials.
Single IA-2 antibody monitored like multiple; single other antibody: repeat every 6 months-3 years.
Adults with T1D-overlap features: standardized islet autoantibody testing.
Screen asymptomatic adults with risk assessment or validated calculator.
Test adults of any age with overweight/obesity and >=1 risk factor.
Everyone else: begin screening at age 35.
Repeat at least every 3 years if normal; sooner with symptoms/weight gain.
FPG, 2-h OGTT and A1C are each acceptable screening tests.
Ensure >=150 g/day carbohydrate for 3 days before OGTT.
Screen overweight/obese youth with risk factors after puberty or age 10.
Consider screening on statins, thiazides, some HIV drugs.
Second-generation antipsychotics: screen at baseline, 12-16 weeks, then annually.
FPG before/at switch and 3-6 months after ART start, then annually.
Monitor postprandial or random glucose with recurrent/long-term steroids.
Educate people starting ICIs, PI3K-alpha or mTOR inhibitors about hyperglycemia.
Test glucose before ICI start and at each visit.
Glucose and A1C before; random glucose weekly x2 weeks then every 4 weeks; A1C 3-monthly optional.
Glucose before and at each visit; A1C 3-monthly optional.
Screen for diabetes 3-6 months after acute pancreatitis then annually; annually in chronic pancreatitis.
Annual OGTT screening from age 10 in cystic fibrosis.
If no OGTT: A1C 5.5-6.4% needs OGTT within 3 months; >=6.5% consistent with CFRD.
Annual complication screening from 5 years after CFRD diagnosis.
Screen for hyperglycemia after transplant; diagnose when stable on immunosuppression, no acute infection.
OGTT is preferred diagnostic test.
Use best immunosuppression for graft regardless of PTDM risk.
Genetic testing for anyone diagnosed in first 6 months of life.
Genetic testing for atypical diabetes with multigenerational family history.
Consult a diabetes-genetics center.
Screen at-risk people planning pregnancy; consider testing all of childbearing potential.
Before 15 weeks test at-risk (consider all) for undiagnosed diabetes.
Before 15 weeks flag A1C 5.9-6.4% or FPG 110-125 as abnormal glucose metabolism.
Screen for GDM at 24-28 weeks.
75-g OGTT at 4-12 weeks postpartum.
Lifelong screening every 1-3 years after GDM.
Assess by A1C and/or CGM metrics (TIR, TAR, TBR); fructosamine or CGM if A1C unreliable.
At least twice yearly; every 3 months if goals unmet, treatment change, hypoglycemia, health change.
A1C <7% (<53 mmol/mol) for many nonpregnant adults without significant hypoglycemia.
CGM time in range 70-180 mg/dL >70%.
Time <70 mg/dL <4% (<1% older adults); <54 mg/dL <1%; deintensify if not met.
Lower A1C goal (<6.5%) if good health/function and low treatment risk.
Less stringent goals with cognitive/functional limits, frailty, severe comorbidity or treatment harm.
Deintensify or switch hypoglycemia-causing drugs in high-risk individuals.
Deintensify when treatment burden/harm exceeds benefit.
Reassess goals using individualized criteria.
Set a glycemic goal during consultation.
Review hypoglycemia history at every visit in at-risk people.
Screen annually for impaired hypoglycemia awareness; refer for intervention.
Screen high-risk for fear of hypoglycemia annually.
Consider hypoglycemia risk when choosing drugs and goals.
CGM recommended in high hypoglycemia risk.
Glucose preferred for glucose <70 mg/dL; avoid fat/protein foods; repeat after 15 min if persists.
Prescribe glucagon to insulin users/high risk; train contacts; prefer ready-to-use.
First-aid kits should contain oral glucose.
Structured hypoglycemia education for insulin users and at-risk people.
One or more level 2/3 episodes: reevaluate and deintensify/switch.
Assess cognition; raise hypoglycemia vigilance if impaired.
Review DKA/HHS history at every visit in at-risk people.
Structured education on crisis recognition/prevention for T1D and high-risk.
Measure BP at every routine visit or at least every 6 months; confirm with multiple readings; hypertension >=130/80.
Teach home BP monitoring.
Individualize BP goal by shared decision-making.
Goal <130/80 if safe; SBP <120 encouraged in high CV or kidney risk.
BP >120/80: weight loss, DASH-style eating, less sodium/alcohol, activity, stop smoking.
Start and titrate drugs for confirmed office BP >=130/80.
BP >=150/90: start two drugs or single-pill combination.
Use classes proven to reduce CV events; ACEi/ARB first-line with albuminuria or CAD.
Multiple drugs usually needed; never combine ACEi, ARB and renin inhibitor.
ACEi/ARB for UACR 30-299; strongly for UACR >=300 or eGFR <60, to maximally tolerated dose.
Check eGFR and potassium at start and periodically with ACEi/ARB/MRA; potassium with diuretics at 7-14 days.
Avoid ACEi, ARB, MRA, renin and neprilysin inhibitors in sexually active people of childbearing potential without reliable contraception.
Add MRA if not at goal on three classes including a diuretic.
Weight loss, Mediterranean/DASH, less saturated/trans fat, more n-3, fibre, stanols, activity.
Triglycerides >=150 or low HDL: intensify lifestyle and glycemic control.
Lipid profile at diagnosis, initial evaluation, then at least annually when not on lipid drugs.
Lipid profile at statin start, 4-12 weeks after change, then annually.
Age 40-75 without ASCVD: moderate-intensity statin.
Age 20-39 with extra ASCVD risk factors: statin may be reasonable.
Age 40-75 with >=1 extra risk factor: high-intensity statin, LDL <70 mg/dL and >=50% reduction.
LDL still >=70 on max statin in higher risk: may add ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitor.
Age >75 already on statin: continue.
Age >75 not on statin: may start moderate-intensity after discussion.
Statin-intolerant: bempedoic acid.
Stop lipid drugs before conception/avoid without contraception; exceptions (FH, prior ASCVD).
ASCVD at any age: high-intensity statin.
ASCVD: LDL <55 mg/dL and >=50% reduction; add ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitor if not met.
Use maximum tolerated statin if intended intensity not tolerated.
ASCVD + statin intolerance: PCSK9 mAb, bempedoic acid or inclisiran.
Fasting TG >=500: look for secondary causes; consider drug therapy to prevent pancreatitis.
TG >150: treat lifestyle, secondary causes, and offending drugs.
On statin with TG 150-499 and ASCVD/risk factors: consider icosapent ethyl.
On statin: do not add fibrate, niacin or n-3 supplements for CV benefit.
Aspirin 75-162 mg/day for secondary prevention.
Aspirin allergy: clopidogrel 75 mg/day.
Duration of dual antiplatelet therapy decided with cardiology/neurology.
Stable CAD/PAD with low bleeding risk: aspirin 81 mg + rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily.
Primary prevention aspirin only in increased CV risk after benefit-bleeding discussion.
No routine CAD screening in asymptomatic people.
Investigate CAD if symptoms/signs, carotid bruit, TIA, stroke, claudication, PAD, ECG abnormalities.
Consider BNP/NT-proBNP screening to detect stage B heart failure.
Abnormal natriuretic peptide: echocardiography.
ABI if age >=65, microvascular disease, foot complications or end-organ damage.
T2D with ASCVD or CKD: SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA with proven benefit.
Combination SGLT2i + GLP-1 RA may be considered for additive benefit.
T2D with HF (any EF): SGLT2i with proven benefit.
T2D CKD with albuminuria on max ACEi/ARB: nonsteroidal MRA.
Age >=55 with ASCVD/multiple risk factors: ACEi or ARB.
Asymptomatic stage B HF: interprofessional GDMT, ACEi/ARB + beta-blocker, SGLT inhibitor.
T2D + obesity + symptomatic HFpEF: dual GIP/GLP-1 RA or GLP-1 RA.
T2D + CKD: nonsteroidal MRA reduces HF hospitalization.
Stage C HF: ACEi/ARB/ARNI, MRA, beta-blocker, SGLT2i; HF with EF >40%: nonsteroidal MRA (not with steroidal MRA).
Metformin may continue in stable HF if eGFR >30; avoid if unstable/hospitalized.
Educate and give ketone tools to SGLT-inhibitor users at DKA risk.
UACR and eGFR at least annually in T1D >=5 years and all T2D.
CKD: UACR and eGFR 1-4 times a year by stage.
Aim to reduce albuminuria >=30% when UACR >=300 mg/g.
CKD G3+: protein 0.8 g/kg/day; dialysis 1.0-1.2 g/kg/day.
Optimize glucose management to prevent/slow CKD.
CKD BP goal <130/80; SBP <120 and less BP variability encouraged.
ACEi or ARB for UACR 30-299; strongly for >=300 or eGFR <60; maximally tolerated dose.
Check eGFR and potassium at start and periodically.
Not for primary CKD prevention with normal BP, UACR and eGFR.
Continue RAS blockade if creatinine rises <=30% without volume depletion.
T2D + CKD: SGLT2i, start if eGFR >=20, continue until kidney failure.
T2D + CKD: GLP-1 RA with proven benefit.
Albuminuric CKD: nonsteroidal MRA if eGFR >=25; check potassium 1 month after start.
Consider starting SGLT2i + finerenone together if UACR >=100 mg/g and eGFR 30-90 on RAS inhibitor.
Avoid harmful kidney-protective drugs without reliable contraception; switch before conception.
eGFR <20 not on dialysis: SGLT2i can continue.
On dialysis: GLP-1-based therapy not dependent on kidney clearance can be started/continued.
Refer to nephrology if rapidly rising UACR, rapidly falling eGFR, or eGFR <30.
Refer if etiology uncertain or difficult management.
Reach glycemic goals to reduce retinopathy risk/progression.
Reach BP and lipid goals to reduce retinopathy risk.
T1D: first dilated comprehensive eye exam 5 years after onset.
T2D: exam at diagnosis.
No retinopathy and goals met: every 1-2 years; any retinopathy: at least annually.
Retinal photography with remote reading or FDA-approved AI is acceptable screening.
Counsel pregnant/planning people with preexisting diabetes on retinopathy risk.
Eye exam before pregnancy, first trimester, then each trimester/1 year postpartum as needed.
Prompt ophthalmology referral for any DME, moderate or worse NPDR, or any PDR.
Panretinal photocoagulation for high-risk PDR and some severe NPDR.
Anti-VEGF is an alternative to laser for some PDR.
Anti-VEGF first-line for center-involved DME with reduced vision.
Focal/grid laser or intravitreal steroid for persistent DME or anti-VEGF-ineligible.
Retinopathy is not a contraindication to aspirin.
Counsel on vision rehabilitation after vision loss.
Provide eye-care support materials with self-management education.
Assess for DPN at T2D diagnosis, 5 years after T1D, then annually.
History plus temperature/pinprick and 128-Hz vibration; annual 10-g monofilament.
Screen autonomic neuropathy symptoms annually.
Optimize glucose, weight, BP and lipids to prevent/slow neuropathy.
Assess and treat neuropathic pain and autonomic symptoms.
Gabapentinoids, SNRIs, TCAs, sodium-channel blockers first-line; avoid opioids/tramadol/tapentadol.
Comprehensive foot evaluation at least annually.
Skin, deformity, monofilament/Ipswich + one other test, vascular exam.
Inspect feet every visit if sensory loss, ulcer or amputation history.
Ask about ulcer, amputation, Charcot, revascularization, smoking, retinopathy, kidney disease, symptoms.
Pulse/capillary refill screen; refer for ABI with toe pressures if suggestive.
Podiatrist-led interprofessional care for ulcers and high-risk feet.
Smokers with prior complications/LOPS/PAD: foot specialist and cessation counseling.
Teach daily foot self-inspection.
Therapeutic footwear for high-risk feet.
Chronic non-healing ulcers: adjunctive advanced therapy (NPWT, skin substitutes, topical oxygen).

drug_classes.name: Biguanide (metformin)
adverse: GI intolerance (bloating, abdominal discomfort, diarrhea): slow titration, extended-release, take with food
Vitamin B12 deficiency: periodic B12 testing
Lactic acidosis very rare, mainly eGFR <30 or overdose/acute kidney injury
monitoring: Vitamin B12 periodically (annually if >4 years or at risk)
drug_classes.notes: Historically first-line; inexpensive; IR twice daily or ER once daily.

drug_classes.name: SGLT2 inhibitors
adverse: DKA incl. euglycemic (rare in T2D; contraindicated in T1D use; avoid after DKA)
Stop 3-4 days before scheduled surgery, during critical illness or prolonged fasting
monitoring: Ketone testing tools (beta-hydroxybutyrate) if DKA risk
drug_classes.notes: Use for HF, CKD, ASCVD irrespective of A1C. Avoid ketogenic/very-low-carb diets and heavy alcohol.

drug_classes.name: GLP-1 receptor agonists
drug_classes.mace: benefit: dulaglutide, liraglutide, semaglutide (SC and oral); neutral: exenatide QW, lixisenatide
drug_classes.hf: benefit: semaglutide (SC) in HFpEF with obesity
drug_classes.ckd_progression: benefit for kidney endpoints: dulaglutide, liraglutide, semaglutide; semaglutide SC shown to slow CKD progression
adverse: Nausea/vomiting/diarrhea (esp. at start and dose increases): smaller meals, stop eating when full, avoid high-fat/spicy food, slower titration
Pancreatitis reported (do not start if high risk; stop if suspected)
Thyroid C-cell tumors in rodents (human relevance undetermined); check product label
Hold before procedures (aspiration risk with anesthesia/sedation)
May impair absorption of oral drugs incl. oral contraceptives during titration
monitoring: Kidney function if severe GI effects
drug_classes.notes: Preferred over insulin as first injectable when no severe hyperglycemia. Do not combine with DPP-4i.

drug_classes.name: Dual GIP/GLP-1 RA (tirzepatide)
adverse: GI effects as for GLP-1 RA
Reduces oral contraceptive exposure: use a second contraceptive method on start/each dose increase until maintenance dose used >=4 weeks
Same class warnings as GLP-1 RA (pancreatitis, gallbladder, retinopathy, aspiration)
monitoring: Kidney function if severe GI effects
drug_classes.notes: Highest glucose and weight efficacy with semaglutide.

drug_classes.name: DPP-4 inhibitors
drug_classes.notes: Never combine with GLP-1 RA or dual agonist. Can be used for mild post-transplant hyperglycemia.

drug_classes.name: Thiazolidinedione (pioglitazone)
adverse: Fluid retention/HF: do not use in HF
Bladder cancer: avoid in active; caution in prior
Low dose may be better tolerated
drug_classes.notes: Option for MASH (alone or with GLP-1 RA) and post-stroke insulin resistance.

drug_classes.name: Sulfonylureas (2nd generation)
adverse: Hypoglycemia (esp. with insulin, CKD, older age)
Glimepiride shown CV-safe; glyburide avoid in CKD; start glipizide/glimepiride conservatively
drug_classes.notes: Low cost; reduce/stop when adding GLP-1 RA, SGLT2i or insulin.

drug_classes.name: Human insulin (regular, NPH, premixed 70/30)
adverse: Hypoglycemia (nocturnal with NPH; delayed post-meal with regular)
drug_classes.notes: Least costly insulins.

drug_classes.name: Insulin analogs (basal long-acting, rapid, ultra-rapid) and inhaled insulin
adverse: Inhaled insulin: FEV1 decline; contraindicated in chronic lung disease; not for smokers/recent quitters; spirometry before and after start
drug_classes.notes: Preferred in T1D. Degludec/glargine U-300 lower nocturnal hypoglycemia than glargine U-100.

drug_classes.name: Other agents (alpha-glucosidase inhibitors, meglitinides, bile acid sequestrant, bromocriptine, pramlintide)
drug_classes.notes: Add-on options if preferred drugs unavailable/not tolerated.

drug_classes.name: ACE inhibitors / ARBs
adverse: Do not combine ACEi + ARB (or + renin inhibitor)
monitoring: eGFR and potassium at start, after titration and periodically
drug_classes.notes: First-line for hypertension with albuminuria or CAD; titrate to maximally tolerated dose.

drug_classes.name: Nonsteroidal MRA (finerenone)
adverse: Hyperkalemia (potassium must be <=4.8 mmol/L to start)
Do not combine with steroidal MRA
monitoring: Potassium 1 month after start and periodically
drug_classes.notes: For T2D with CKD and albuminuria on max ACEi/ARB, eGFR >=25; reduces CKD progression and HF hospitalization.

drug_classes.name: Statins
adverse: Small increase in diabetes risk (benefit far exceeds risk; do not stop)
Myopathy; higher risk with fibrate (esp. gemfibrozil) or renal insufficiency
Avoid in pregnancy/without contraception (exceptions: FH, prior ASCVD)
monitoring: Lipid panel before, 4-12 weeks after start/dose change, then annually
drug_classes.notes: Moderate-intensity age 40-75; high-intensity if extra risk factors or ASCVD.

drug_classes.name: Ezetimibe
drug_classes.notes: Add to maximally tolerated statin if LDL goal not met.

drug_classes.name: PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab, alirocumab; inclisiran siRNA)
adverse: Injection-site reactions; monoclonal antibodies preferred over inclisiran until outcome trials
drug_classes.notes: Add if LDL goal unmet on max statin (+ezetimibe) or statin intolerance with ASCVD.

drug_classes.name: Bempedoic acid
drug_classes.notes: Statin intolerance: lowers LDL ~15-24% and reduces MACE.

drug_classes.name: Icosapent ethyl
adverse: Do not extrapolate to other n-3 products
drug_classes.notes: On statin with TG 150-499 and ASCVD/risk factors.

drug_classes.name: Aspirin / antiplatelets
drug_classes.notes: 75-162 mg/day secondary prevention; primary prevention only selected high CV risk, low bleeding risk (generally not >70 y).

drug_classes.name: Low-dose rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily (with aspirin 81 mg)
drug_classes.notes: Stable CAD/PAD, low bleeding risk.

drug_classes.name: Neuropathic pain drugs (gabapentinoids, SNRIs, TCAs, sodium-channel blockers, topical capsaicin/lidocaine)
adverse: Gabapentinoids: dizziness/sedation, start low go slow
drug_classes.notes: Combination of 2-3 agents at lower doses may help.

drug_classes.name: Glucagon products
adverse: Teach contacts: never give insulin during hypoglycemia
drug_classes.notes: Prefer ready-to-use or nasal forms.

insulin_cost_per_1000_units.product: degludec/liraglutide fixed-ratio pen (per 1,000 units basis as listed)

insulin_dosing.guidance: Typical 0.4-1 unit/kg/day; 0.5 unit/kg/day typical start in metabolically stable adults; newly diagnosed adults 0.2-0.6 unit/kg/day; higher in puberty, late luteal phase, illness.
About 30-50% of TDD basal, remainder prandial.
Choose evidence-based algorithm, e.g., increase 2 units every 3 days to reach fasting glucose goal without hypoglycemia. If hypoglycemia: find cause; if none, lower dose 10-20%.
4 units or 10% of basal dose with the largest meal / greatest post-meal excursion; then stepwise add doses.
Increase 1-2 units or 10-15% twice weekly; for hypoglycemia determine cause, else reduce 10-20%.
Often unit-for-unit; reduce 10-20% when tight control/high hypoglycemia risk and when switching from NPH or U-300 glargine.
One approach: total NPH = 80% of current bedtime dose, 2/3 morning and 1/3 bedtime.
Bedtime-to-morning glucose differential >=50 mg/dL (>=2.8 mmol/L), postprandial-to-preprandial differential, hypoglycemia, high variability: reassess and address prandial needs.
When adding substantial prandial insulin (esp. evening) consider reducing basal.
4-mm pen needles lower risk of intramuscular injection; rotate sites; avoid lipohypertrophy.
Indications: symptoms, A1C >10%, glucose >=300 mg/dL, catabolism; consider GLP-1 RA first otherwise; continue metformin/SGLT2i/GLP-1 RA; limit sulfonylurea/meglitinide/DPP-4i.
If A1C >=1.5% above goal many need dual therapy or a more potent agent; each added oral class lowers A1C ~0.7-1.0%; GLP-1 RA/tirzepatide ~1% to >=2%.

rules.title: ASCVD or high CV risk
recommend: GLP1RA (proven CV benefit: dulaglutide, liraglutide, semaglutide)
SGLT2I (proven CV benefit: canagliflozin, empagliflozin)
rules.note: Independent of A1C and of metformin use; consider initial GLP-1 RA + SGLT2i combination.

rules.title: Heart failure
recommend: SGLT2I (canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, ertugliflozin)

rules.title: Symptomatic HFpEF with obesity
recommend: TIRZEPATIDE
GLP1RA semaglutide

rules.title: CKD eGFR 20-60 and/or albuminuria
recommend: SGLT2I (empagliflozin, canagliflozin, dapagliflozin)
GLP1RA with CKD benefit (semaglutide first)
rules.note: SGLT2i glucose lowering weak at eGFR <45; still use for kidney/CV benefit if eGFR >=20.

rules.title: Advanced CKD eGFR <30
recommend: GLP1RA (dulaglutide, liraglutide, semaglutide: no dose adjustment)
rules.note: Insulin/sulfonylurea: high hypoglycemia risk, lower doses, close monitoring.

rules.title: Metformin: do not start if eGFR <45
Metformin: reduce dose eGFR <45, stop <30
flags: Reduce metformin dose when eGFR <45; STOP if eGFR <30.

rules.title: Obesity / weight goal
recommend: Semaglutide or tirzepatide (highest weight loss)
Then dulaglutide/liraglutide
SGLT2I modest loss

rules.title: MASLD/MASH
recommend: GLP1RA (semaglutide approved for MASH with moderate-advanced fibrosis)
TIRZEPATIDE
Pioglitazone (alone or with GLP-1 RA)

rules.title: Decompensated cirrhosis
recommend: Insulin

rules.title: Initial combination therapy
recommend: Dual combination or more potent agent (GLP-1 RA/tirzepatide, insulin)

rules.title: Severe hyperglycemia / catabolic
recommend: Consider basal insulin (+/- prandial); add GLP-1 RA/tirzepatide; simplify later as glucotoxicity resolves

rules.title: Prefer GLP-1 RA before insulin if no severe hyperglycemia
recommend: GLP1RA or TIRZEPATIDE before starting insulin

rules.title: Insulin: combine with GLP-1 RA
recommend: Add GLP1RA/TIRZEPATIDE (fixed-ratio products available)
rules.note: Reassess insulin dose on GLP-1 RA start/escalation.

rules.title: Starting insulin: continue other agents
flags: Continue metformin, SGLT2i, GLP-1 RA; reduce/stop sulfonylurea, meglitinide, DPP-4i.

rules.title: Glucagon for insulin users
recommend: Prescribe glucagon (no-reconstitution product preferred); train family/caregivers

rules.title: CGM
recommend: Offer CGM; consider AID system if on insulin (9.27)

rules.title: DPP-4i + GLP-1 RA
flags: Stop DPP-4 inhibitor: no added benefit.

rules.title: Reassess hypoglycemia-prone drugs
flags: When adding a new agent, reassess need/dose of sulfonylurea/meglitinide/insulin to avoid hypoglycemia.

rules.title: History of pancreatitis
recommend: Early insulin

rules.title: Gallbladder disease
flags: Avoid GLP-1 RA in at-risk individuals; evaluate if cholelithiasis/cholecystitis suspected.

rules.title: GLP-1 RA and retinopathy
flags: Close eye monitoring; monitor for NAION.

rules.title: DKA risk with SGLT2i
rules.note: Contraindicated/not approved in T1D; do not use after DKA.

rules.title: SGLT2i + ketogenic/very-low-carb diet, fasting, or heavy alcohol
flags: Avoid ketogenic/very-low-carb eating and excess alcohol; ensure hydration; provide ketone testing; do not start SGLT2i close to fasting days.

rules.title: SGLT2i before surgery
flags: Stop SGLT2i 3-4 days before scheduled surgery.

rules.title: GLP-1 RA before anesthesia
flags: Give peri-procedural guidance on holding (aspiration risk).

rules.title: Pioglitazone in HF
flags: Pioglitazone increases HF risk: do not use.

rules.title: Pioglitazone and bladder cancer/fractures
flags: Avoid pioglitazone in active bladder cancer; caution prior history; fracture risk.

rules.title: Inhaled insulin and lung disease
flags: Spirometry (FEV1) needed before/after starting inhaled insulin.

rules.title: Cost barrier
recommend: Metformin
Sulfonylurea (glimepiride/glipizide; avoid glyburide in CKD)
Pioglitazone
Human insulin (regular/NPH/70-30)
rules.note: Weigh hypoglycemia, weight gain, CV/kidney risk of cheaper drugs.

rules.title: Shortage / compounded incretins
flags: Do not prescribe/accept compounded semaglutide/tirzepatide; switch to approved alternative in shortage and reassess later.

rules.title: Tirzepatide and oral contraceptives
flags: Use second contraceptive method until maintenance dose reached and used >=4 weeks (and after dose escalations).

rules.title: Childbearing potential counseling
flags: Review all drugs for pregnancy safety; preconception planning several months ahead; use pregnancy-approved therapy (see Section 15).

rules.title: Immune checkpoint inhibitor hyperglycemia
recommend: Assess for immediate insulin (consider basal insulin if glucose >250 mg/dL); do not stop ICI
flags: DKA risk; usually lifelong insulin

rules.title: PI3K-alpha inhibitor hyperglycemia
recommend: Metformin first-line (consider prophylactic start 1 week before)
Pioglitazone or SGLT2i (monitor ketoacidosis) next

rules.title: mTOR inhibitor hyperglycemia
recommend: Metformin first-line
Pioglitazone second-line
Insulin if refractory/severe

rules.title: Glucocorticoid hyperglycemia
recommend: Insulin most used (match timing; NPH morning for AM prednisone); sulfonylurea/meglitinide alternatives
Metformin prophylaxis in high-risk (Sec 3)
flags: Monitor afternoon/evening glucose, not only fasting; adjust as steroid tapers.

rules.title: Transplant recipient
recommend: Early postoperative: insulin; mild: DPP-4i
Long term: GLP-1 RA, SGLT2i (UTI risk), metformin (eGFR >=45 to start; stop <30)

rules.title: Second-generation antipsychotics
flags: Monitor weight, glucose, lipids every 12-16 weeks.

rules.title: Metformin B12 monitoring
flags: Check vitamin B12 (annually if >4 years metformin or at risk).

rules.title: Prediabetes: metformin consideration
recommend: Lifestyle (DPP: 5-7% weight loss, 150 min/week) first-line
Consider metformin; consider GLP-1/tirzepatide for obesity

rules.title: Prediabetes monitoring
flags: Test for progression at least annually; address CV risk factors; do not stop statins.

rules.title: Statin and diabetes risk
flags: Monitor glucose regularly; statin should NOT be stopped for this reason.

rules.title: Prior stroke with insulin resistance
recommend: Consider pioglitazone
flags: Weigh weight gain, edema, fractures.

rules.title: Presymptomatic T1D
flags: A1C ~6-monthly and OGTT annually; discuss teplizumab for stage 2 T1D age >=8 years.

rules.title: Type 1 diabetes plan
recommend: Basal-bolus analog insulin or pump/AID
CGM
Glucagon
Carb counting + correction education

rules.title: Religious fasting planned
flags: Perform IDF-DAR risk score well in advance; adjust therapy (see fasting_adjustments); fasting-focused education.

rules.title: Tobacco/vaping
recommend: Counseling + pharmacotherapy (varenicline most effective in diabetes data)

rules.title: Disordered eating
flags: Refer to behavioral health; avoid rigid carb counting/intensive weight monitoring; check for insulin omission or dose reduction to control weight; review drugs affecting hunger.

rules.title: Very-low-carbohydrate diet cautions
flags: Medical oversight; adjust insulin/secretagogue to prevent hypoglycemia; not recommended in pregnancy, children, kidney disease, disordered eating.

rules.title: Food insecurity
flags: Avoid hypoglycemia-prone drugs where food access unreliable; refer to food resources.

rules.title: A1C unreliable: use plasma glucose
flags: Use plasma glucose criteria (or fructosamine/CGM for monitoring); A1C may be misleading.

rules.title: Features suggest type 1 diabetes
flags: Consider T1D: test islet autoantibodies (GAD first) and C-peptide if insulin-treated; do not delay insulin.

rules.title: Possible monogenic diabetes
flags: Offer genetic testing; consult diabetes genetics center.

rules.title: Cystic fibrosis screening
flags: Annual OGTT from age 10.

rules.title: SGA antipsychotic glucose screening
flags: Glucose screen at baseline, 12-16 weeks, then annually.

rules.title: HIV glucose screening
flags: FPG before/after ART change (3-6 months), then annually.

rules.title: ICI glucose monitoring
flags: Glucose at each visit and with symptoms.

rules.title: Islet autoantibody positive
flags: Test for stage 3 T1D (A1C, glucose, urinalysis); multiple antibodies: specialist referral, teplizumab discussion.

rules.title: Level 2/3 hypoglycemia
flags: Reevaluate regimen now: deintensify or switch to lower-hypoglycemia drug; relax goal temporarily; CGM; glucagon; structured education.

rules.title: Impaired hypoglycemia awareness
flags: Use CGM; several weeks of avoiding hypoglycemia (temporarily higher goals) can restore awareness; refer for awareness training.

rules.title: CGM time below range above target
flags: Time below range above target: deintensify or modify therapy.

rules.title: High glucose variability
flags: CV >36% associated with hypoglycemia; review dosing/timing.

rules.title: Time above range high
flags: Time >250 mg/dL above 5% target: intensify/adjust.

rules.title: Older adult / limited life expectancy goals
flags: Use less stringent goals (A1C <8%; CGM TIR >50%, <70 mg/dL <1%); prioritize avoiding hypoglycemia; deintensify if harms exceed benefit.

rules.title: Acute illness with poor intake
flags: Consider holding metformin and SGLT2i; hold GLP-1 RA if significant GI symptoms; never stop basal insulin; check glucose and ketones more often.

rules.title: Sulfonylurea + interacting antimicrobial
flags: Fluoroquinolone/clarithromycin/TMP-SMX/metronidazole/fluconazole can precipitate hypoglycemia: reduce or temporarily stop sulfonylurea.

rules.title: Check ketones
flags: Measure blood ketones (BHB); urgent care if vomiting, ketones/glucose not improving, altered mental state.

rules.title: Raised ketones
flags: Beta-hydroxybutyrate >=0.8 mmol/L increases DKA risk (SGLT inhibitor data): treat per sick-day plan and contact care team.

rules.title: Rapid A1C reduction
flags: Rapid glucose lowering can transiently worsen retinopathy: examine eyes when intensifying (esp. GLP-1 RA).

rules.title: Start antihypertensive therapy
recommend: Lifestyle (DASH, sodium, weight, activity) + drug therapy titrated to <130/80 (SBP <120 if high CV/kidney risk)
flags: Confirm on >=2 occasions; home BP monitoring

rules.title: BP >=150/90: two drugs
recommend: Start two agents or a single-pill combination (ACEi/ARB + dihydropyridine CCB or thiazide-like diuretic)

rules.title: ACEi/ARB indicated
recommend: ACEi or ARB at maximally tolerated dose (strongly if UACR >=300 or eGFR <60)
flags: Check eGFR and potassium at start/titration; diuretic potassium at 7-14 days.

rules.title: Dual RAS blockade
flags: No added benefit; more hyperkalemia, AKI, syncope: stop one.

rules.title: RAS blockers/MRAs and pregnancy
flags: Contraindicated in pregnancy: switch before conception (methyldopa, labetalol, long-acting nifedipine are options); reliable contraception.

rules.title: Resistant hypertension
recommend: Add MRA; screen secondary causes (aldosteronism, renal artery stenosis, OSA); check adherence
flags: Monitor potassium/creatinine.

rules.title: Hyperkalemia with RAS/MRA
flags: Review potassium, diet, interacting drugs; do not start finerenone if K >4.8 mmol/L.

rules.title: Creatinine rise <=30% on RAS blocker
flags: Do NOT stop ACEi/ARB for creatinine rise <=30% without volume depletion.

rules.title: Statin: primary prevention age 40-75
recommend: Moderate-intensity statin; HIGH-intensity (LDL <70 mg/dL, >=50% reduction) if >=1 extra ASCVD risk factor (older age, hypertension, dyslipidemia, smoking, CKD, obesity)
If LDL >=70 on maximum statin: consider ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitor

rules.title: Statin age 20-39 with risk factors
recommend: Statin may be reasonable (moderate-intensity; discuss; contraception if childbearing)

rules.title: Statin age >75
recommend: Continue statin if already on it; if not, moderate-intensity may be started after risk-benefit discussion

rules.title: Statin: ASCVD
recommend: High-intensity statin: LDL <55 mg/dL and >=50% reduction
Add ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitor if goal not met on maximum tolerated statin

rules.title: LDL above secondary-prevention goal
recommend: Intensify lipid-lowering (max statin, ezetimibe, PCSK9 inhibitor)

rules.title: LDL above primary-prevention high-risk goal
recommend: Consider adding ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitor

rules.title: Statin intolerance
recommend: Use maximum tolerated statin dose (or nondaily dosing)
Add bempedoic acid; with ASCVD also PCSK9 monoclonal antibody (preferred) or inclisiran

rules.title: Severe hypertriglyceridemia
flags: Look for secondary causes (alcohol, glycemia, hypothyroidism, drugs); consider fibrate/fish oil to prevent pancreatitis; reduce fat and alcohol.

rules.title: Residual triglycerides on statin
recommend: Consider icosapent ethyl
flags: Do not add fibrate, niacin or OTC n-3 supplements for CV benefit.

rules.title: Lipid drugs and pregnancy
flags: Stop statin before conception in most cases (exceptions: FH, prior ASCVD event).

rules.title: Aspirin: ASCVD
recommend: Aspirin 75-162 mg/day (clopidogrel 75 mg if aspirin allergy)

rules.title: Aspirin: primary prevention
recommend: May consider aspirin 75-162 mg after shared decision on bleeding risk

rules.title: Aspirin not recommended
flags: Primary-prevention aspirin generally not recommended (age <50 low risk, age >70, or high bleeding risk); aspirin <21 y contraindicated (Reye).

rules.title: Low-dose rivaroxaban + aspirin
recommend: Consider aspirin 81 mg + rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily in stable CAD/PAD (not if systemic anticoagulation or DAPT needed)

rules.title: Heart failure screening
flags: Consider BNP (>=50 pg/mL) or NT-proBNP (>=125 pg/mL) screening; abnormal: echocardiography. Levels may be falsely low in obesity.

rules.title: Abnormal natriuretic peptide
recommend: Echocardiography; if stage B: ACEi/ARB + beta-blocker, SGLT2i, cardiology involvement

rules.title: PAD screening
flags: Ankle-brachial index (with toe pressures) if diagnosis would change management.

rules.title: HF with reduced EF
recommend: ACEi/ARB/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i; metformin only if stable and eGFR >30

rules.title: Kidney screening
flags: UACR and eGFR (CKD-EPI 2021) at least annually; confirm abnormal UACR with 2 of 3 samples in 3-6 months.

rules.title: Nonsteroidal MRA
recommend: Finerenone (on maximally tolerated ACEi/ARB); check potassium at 1 month

rules.title: SGLT2i + finerenone together
recommend: Consider simultaneous SGLT2i + finerenone (CONFIDENCE: UACR -52%)

rules.title: Albuminuria reduction target
flags: Aim for >=30% UACR reduction; titrate ACEi/ARB to maximum tolerated; add SGLT2i, finerenone, GLP-1 RA.

rules.title: Protein intake in CKD
flags: Protein about 0.8 g/kg/day (not lower; avoid >1.3 g/kg/day); sodium <2,300 mg/day; individualize potassium.

rules.title: Dialysis
flags: Protein 1.0-1.2 g/kg/day; GLP-1 RA not cleared by kidney can be used; exenatide/lixisenatide not used.

rules.title: Nephrology referral
flags: Refer to nephrology (eGFR <30, rapidly rising UACR/falling eGFR, atypical features).

rules.title: CKD complication screen & nephrotoxins
flags: Screen anemia, bone-mineral, electrolytes/acidosis (G3 every 6-12 months); verify drug doses; avoid NSAIDs and minimize iodinated contrast; hepatitis B vaccination.

rules.title: NSAID use in CKD
flags: Avoid NSAIDs: risk of acute kidney injury.

rules.title: Consider non-diabetic kidney disease
flags: Atypical features: nephrology evaluation (possible biopsy).

rules.title: Eye exam T2D
flags: Dilated comprehensive eye exam at diagnosis; yearly (every 1-2 years if no retinopathy and goals met).

rules.title: Eye exam T1D
flags: Dilated eye exam now and annually (5 years after onset if not yet done).

rules.title: Retinopathy needs ophthalmologist
flags: Prompt referral to ophthalmologist experienced in diabetic retinopathy; anti-VEGF first-line for center-involved DME; laser/anti-VEGF for PDR.

rules.title: Severe NPDR/PDR and vigorous exercise
flags: Vigorous aerobic or resistance exercise may be contraindicated: check with ophthalmologist.

rules.title: Aspirin with retinopathy
flags: Retinopathy is not a contraindication to aspirin.

rules.title: Eye exams around pregnancy
flags: Eye exam before pregnancy, in the first trimester, then each trimester/1 year postpartum as needed (not required for GDM).

rules.title: Neuropathy screening
flags: Annual neuropathy assessment (pinprick/temperature, 128-Hz vibration, 10-g monofilament); consider B12 deficiency (metformin) and other causes; screen autonomic symptoms.

rules.title: Painful neuropathy
recommend: Gabapentinoid, SNRI (duloxetine), TCA (amitriptyline; caution >=65 y) or sodium-channel blocker; combine at low doses if needed
Topical capsaicin or lidocaine patch if oral drugs unsuitable

rules.title: Orthostatic hypotension
recommend: Salt/fluid adequacy, compression garments, stop aggravating drugs; midodrine or droxidopa if needed
flags: Goal is symptom control; supine hypertension may need bedtime short-acting agent.

rules.title: Gastroparesis symptoms
recommend: Small-particle eating pattern
Review drugs slowing motility (GLP-1 RA, opioids, anticholinergics, TCAs, pramlintide)
flags: Metoclopramide only for severe cases, not beyond 12 weeks (FDA).

rules.title: High-risk foot
flags: Inspect feet every visit if LOPS/ulcer/amputation; refer to podiatry/foot-care team; therapeutic footwear; smoking cessation.

rules.title: Active foot ulcer or infection
flags: Urgent foot-care team: offloading, debridement, infection management, vascular assessment; consider stopping canagliflozin; advanced therapy if <50% area reduction in 4 weeks.

rules.title: SGLT2i and lower-limb complication
flags: Consider stopping canagliflozin (amputation signal in CANVAS) until limb complication resolved.

rules.title: Hot swollen red foot
flags: Suspect Charcot neuroarthropathy: X-ray, strict non-weight-bearing, urgent foot specialist.

instructions.text: Take metformin with meals. Mild stomach upset or loose stools are common at first and usually settle; your dose is increased slowly to help. Tell your doctor if you have vomiting, severe diarrhea, dehydration or kidney problems.
Long-term metformin can lower vitamin B12. Get your B12 level checked regularly; report numbness, tingling or unusual tiredness.
Drink enough water. Keep the genital area clean and dry. Report burning urine, fever, genital pain/swelling, or pain, redness or swelling around the genitals or back passage immediately.
If you are vomiting, not eating or drinking, have severe illness, or are fasting for a long period, stop this tablet and contact your doctor. Stop it 3-4 days before planned surgery.

Avoid very low-carbohydrate or ketogenic diets and heavy alcohol. Seek urgent care for nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fast breathing or unusual tiredness even if your sugar is not very high; check blood ketones if you have a meter.

Eat smaller meals and stop when you feel full; avoid very fatty or spicy food. Nausea usually improves over time. Seek care for severe or persistent abdominal pain (with or without vomiting) or yellowing of skin/eyes. Tell your doctor before any surgery or procedure needing sedation.
Your dose will be increased in steps; do not skip steps or increase on your own. Do not buy compounded or unregulated injectable versions.
Same weekly day each week. If you take birth-control pills, use an additional non-oral method for 4 weeks after starting and after each dose increase.
Report severe, persistent abdominal pain, severe joint pain, or blisters on the skin and stop the medicine until reviewed.
Report weight gain, swollen ankles or breathlessness immediately. Tell your doctor about bone fractures or blood in urine.
Never skip meals while taking this medicine. Carry fast-acting sugar. Learn the signs of low sugar (shaking, sweating, hunger, confusion).
Inject into fat under the skin (abdomen, thigh, buttock, upper arm), rotate sites each time and avoid lumpy areas. Check glucose as advised and do not change your dose on your own unless taught how.
Use short (4 mm) pen needles; new needle each time; rotate sites; avoid injecting into lumps. Match mealtime insulin to carbohydrate as taught, with correction doses when high.

Low sugar (below 70 mg/dL): shaking, sweating, hunger, palpitations, confusion. Take 15 g fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes and repeat if needed, then eat. Tell your doctor about every low.
Keep glucagon (ready-to-use form if possible) at hand. Family and close contacts must know where it is and how to use it for a severe low (unable to swallow or unconscious); call emergency services.
Never stop basal insulin when ill. Check glucose (and ketones) more often, drink fluids, and call your team if ketones are present, you vomit, or sugars stay high.
Use only approved, pharmacy-dispensed products. Avoid compounded or online unregulated versions.
Some diabetes medicines are unsafe in pregnancy or affect birth-control absorption. Use reliable contraception and talk to your doctor months before planning pregnancy.
Kidney function and urine albumin will be checked regularly; avoid unprescribed painkillers (NSAIDs) and stay hydrated.
Have a dilated eye examination at diagnosis and then every 1-2 years (every year if retinopathy is present); go sooner for any sudden vision change.
This medicine protects heart and kidneys as well as lowering sugar. Keep taking it even when sugars are normal.
Aim for at least 5-7% weight loss (more gives more benefit) through reduced-calorie, nutritious eating and regular activity.
While losing weight include muscle-strengthening exercise 2-3 days a week and adequate protein to keep muscle.
Plate method: half non-starchy vegetables, one quarter lean or plant protein, one quarter high-fibre carbohydrate (whole grain/legumes).

Eat vegetables, whole fruit, legumes, whole grains, nuts and seeds; use unsaturated oils; limit red/processed meat, sweets, refined grains, packaged and ultra-processed foods. A Mediterranean-style pattern is a good choice.
Drink water instead of sweetened drinks and juices; unsweetened or no-calorie drinks are acceptable.
Keep sodium below 2,300 mg/day (about 5 g salt): limit processed foods, do not add extra salt.
Choose high-fibre carbohydrates (at least 14 g fibre per 1,000 kcal).
Vitamin, mineral and herbal supplements (cinnamon, chromium, aloe) do not improve sugar control; tell your doctor what you take. Do not take beta-carotene supplements.
If you drink: no more than 1 drink/day (women) or 2 (men), never on an empty stomach. Alcohol can cause delayed low sugar, so check glucose before bed and the next morning.
At least 150 minutes/week of moderate to vigorous activity (e.g., brisk walking) spread over 3 or more days, with no more than 2 days in a row without activity.
Do resistance exercise 2-3 days a week on non-consecutive days; older adults add balance and flexibility work.
Break up long sitting at least every 30 minutes with a short walk or light activity.
Check glucose before and after exercise; low sugar can occur during and hours after. Carry fast-acting carbohydrate; take extra carbohydrate if glucose is below 90 mg/dL before exercising as advised.

Stopping tobacco and vaping lowers your risk of heart, kidney and eye disease. Ask for counseling and medicines to help you quit; weight gain after quitting is usually small and does not cancel the benefit.
Avoid recreational cannabis: it can cause vomiting and ketoacidosis in type 1 diabetes.

Aim for about 7 hours of regular sleep; keep fixed bed and wake times, a dark quiet room, no screens before bed, limit evening caffeine and avoid alcohol before sleep. Tell your doctor if you snore loudly or stop breathing at night.
Join a structured diabetes prevention programme (in-person or certified digital) for coaching on weight loss and activity.
Attend diabetes self-management education and support at diagnosis, yearly, when targets are not met, and after major life or health changes.
See a registered dietitian for an individualized meal plan.
While on steroid tablets/injections check glucose also in the afternoon and evening, not only fasting; doses may need to change as the steroid is reduced.

Before religious fasting, review your treatment plan and risk with your doctor. Check glucose more often (especially the last hours of fasting); break the fast if glucose is below 70 mg/dL or above 300 mg/dL or you feel unwell; drink plenty of fluids and avoid sugary, very fatty meals when breaking the fast.
Medication plan will be reviewed every 3-6 months; do not delay review if targets are not met.
If cost is a problem, tell your doctor or pharmacist: lower-cost effective options exist. Do not stop medicines without advice.

When ill with vomiting, diarrhea or poor intake: keep drinking fluids, check glucose every 3-4 hours, never stop basal insulin, and call your care team about stopping metformin or SGLT2 tablets (and GLP-1 injections if you have stomach symptoms) until you can eat and drink normally.

If glucose is above 200 mg/dL when unwell, check blood ketones. Go to hospital if you cannot keep fluids down, keep vomiting, ketones or sugars do not fall after insulin, or you feel confused or breathless.

Low sugar: take 15 g glucose (3-4 glucose tablets or about 150 mL juice), recheck in 15 minutes, repeat if still below 70 mg/dL, then eat a snack. Do not treat with chocolate or high-fat food first. If you take acarbose use pure glucose. Never give insulin to someone with a low.
Check blood pressure at home sitting, after 5 minutes rest, arm at heart level; keep a log and bring it to visits. Usual goal is below 130/80 mmHg unless your doctor sets another goal.
Follow a DASH-style diet: more fruits, vegetables, low-fat dairy; less salt (below 2,300 mg sodium/day); limit alcohol; stay active.

Do not take this medicine if pregnant or planning pregnancy; tell your doctor immediately. Report dizziness, fainting, swelling of lips/face. Blood tests for kidney function and potassium are needed; avoid potassium supplements and salt substitutes unless advised. Do not stop on your own.
Blood potassium will be checked about 1 month after starting and periodically. Avoid potassium supplements and potassium salt substitutes. Not for use in pregnancy.

Take your statin daily. Report unexplained muscle pain, weakness or dark urine. A cholesterol test will be repeated 4-12 weeks after starting or changing the dose and then yearly. Not for use in pregnancy: tell your doctor if planning a baby.
Take low-dose aspirin daily as prescribed with food. Report black stools, vomiting blood or unusual bleeding. Do not start or stop without advice.
With kidney disease: keep protein at about 0.8 g/kg body weight a day (not very low), limit salt, and follow your dietitian's advice about potassium. Avoid painkillers like ibuprofen or diclofenac.
Avoid anti-inflammatory painkillers (ibuprofen, diclofenac, naproxen) because they can harm your kidneys; ask your pharmacist for safe alternatives.
Nerve-pain medicines work gradually: start low and increase slowly. Tell your doctor about drowsiness, dizziness or stomach upset. Avoid opioid painkillers for nerve pain.

Look at both feet every day (use an unbreakable mirror if needed) for cuts, blisters, redness, swelling or colour change. Wash and dry between toes, moisturize dry skin, never walk barefoot, and do not cut corns or calluses yourself. Report any wound at once.
Wear well-fitting shoes or prescribed therapeutic footwear/insoles; check inside shoes for stones before wearing.
Keep glucagon where family can find it, check the expiry date, and learn how to give it. After giving glucagon call emergency services.
